entry: Folding canopy on ribs and a pole, designed to protect a person against [[Sun|sun]] or [[Rain|rain]]. In warmer countries, umbrellas were used for shade from the sun from the early 1200s and only later for protection from rain. The earliest known umbrellas in Egyptian art date to the Fifth Dynasty, around 2450 BC, typically depicted as a fan-like *flabellum* on a long handle. The word derives from the [[Latin|Latin]] *umbra*, meaning "shadow." There are two main types: completely collapsible umbrellas, which fold because their metal pole retracts, and non-collapsible umbrellas, where only the canopy folds. In Britain, umbrellas were once called *gamps* after Mrs. Gamp in [[Charles Dickens|Charles Dickens]]'s novel *Martin Chuzzlewit*.

Egyptian singer and film actress. She was given the honorific title *Kawkab el-Sharq* ("Planet of the East") and was dubbed "The Voice of Egypt." Born in the village of Tamay al-Zahayra in the Dakahlia Governorate, she sang religious hymns as a child with her father, who dressed her in boys' clothes because singing was unacceptable for girls in the countryside. After moving to [[Cairo|Cairo]] in the early 1920s, she became known for her powerful contralto voice and long, complex songs, and she was active from the 1920s to the 1970s. After the 1967 war she gave concerts in Arab and European countries to raise funds for the Egyptian war effort. Her funeral in Cairo drew over 4 million people. In 2023, [[Rolling Stone|Rolling Stone]] ranked her number 61 on its list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time.

Hypothesis that an almost-human entity provokes eerie or repellent feelings. Proposed by robotics professor Masahiro Mori in 1970, it holds that as a figure becomes more humanlike, viewer responses grow more positive until near-perfect resemblance triggers strong revulsion, then turn positive again as the figure becomes indistinguishable from a human. Examples exist among [[Robot|robots]], animatronics, [[Doll|lifelike dolls]], and [[Computer animation|computer animation]]. Empirical support is mixed.

Fundamental limit in [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] on how precisely certain paired properties can be known together. Also called Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, it states that the more accurately one property, such as position, is measured, the less accurately its complementary property, such as [[Momentum|momentum]], can be known. German physicist [[Werner Heisenberg]] introduced it in 1927. Earle Hesse Kennard derived the formal inequality, relating the standard deviations of position and momentum, later that year, and [[Hermann Weyl]] did so in 1928. In wave mechanics, the relation arises because the position and momentum wavefunctions are [[Fourier transform|Fourier transforms]] of each other, and a nonzero function and its Fourier transform cannot both be sharply localized. The principle extends to other pairs, such as energy and time. Its effects are significant only for microscopic objects and negligible for macroscopic ones.

Anti-slavery novel by American author Harriet Beecher Stowe. Stowe wrote it in response to the second Fugitive Slave Act, passed in 1850. It first appeared as a serial in the abolitionist newspaper *The National Era* from June 5, 1851, and was published in two volumes in 1852. The novel centers on Uncle Tom, a long-suffering enslaved man, and asserts that Christian love could overcome [[Slavery|slavery]]. It was the best-selling novel in the United States in the 19th century and the second best-selling book after the Bible, and it is said to have helped lay the groundwork for the [[American Civil War|American Civil War]]. An apocryphal story has [[Abraham Lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] greeting Stowe as "the little lady who started this great war." The book and the plays it inspired popularized negative [[Stereotype|stereotypes]] of Black people, and "Uncle Tom" came to mean an excessively subservient person.

Segment of the population occupying the lowest possible position in a class hierarchy, below the core of the [[Working class|working class]]. The idea of a population beneath the working class has a long tradition in the social sciences, as in the *lumpenproletariat*, but the specific term was popularized in the last half of the 20th century, first by social scientists of American [[Poverty|poverty]] and then by American journalists. Writing in the early 1960s, Gunnar Myrdal is generally credited as the first proponent of the term. He described an underclass as a "class of unemployed, unemployables, and underemployed" set apart from the nation at large. According to sociologist Herbert Gans, many journalists and academics later replaced this structural conception with a behavioral one that fused Myrdal's term with Oscar Lewis's "culture of poverty." The concept remains controversial, and its definitions and remedies are highly debated.

Practice of descending below the water's surface to interact with the environment. Immersion and high [[Pressure|ambient pressure]] limit the depths and durations humans can reach, so equipment has been developed to extend them. Breath-hold diving, or freediving, goes back at least to classical times. Self-contained breathing systems developed at an accelerated rate after the Second World War, and scuba and surface-supplied diving use breathing apparatus. Saturation diving reduces the risk of decompression sickness (DCS) after long, deep dives. Recreational scuba diving is restricted to maximum depths of about 40 meters (130 ft), commercial saturation diving to 530 meters (1,740 ft), and diving in atmospheric suits to 610 meters (2,000 ft). Diving remains a relatively dangerous activity. Professional diving is usually regulated by occupational health and safety law, while recreational diving may be entirely unregulated.

Clothing worn beneath outer clothes, usually in direct contact with the skin. Underwear keeps outer garments from being soiled by bodily excretions, lessens [[Friction|friction]] against outerwear, shapes the body, and provides concealment or support. Women's [[Bra|bras]] support the breasts, and sports bras reduce the chance of damage to the [[Ligament|ligaments]] of the chest during high-impact exercise such as jogging. Men commonly wear boxer briefs or boxer shorts, while women often wear bras and panties. Items worn by both sexes include T-shirts, singlets, classic briefs, and [[Bikini|bikini]] briefs. In cold weather, long underwear adds warmth, and some underwear can serve as [[Nightwear|nightwear]]. Some undergarments are intended for sexual attraction or visual appeal, and some have religious significance.

State of being without paid employment or self-employment while available for work. Unemployment is measured by the unemployment rate, the number of unemployed people as a percentage of the labor force. Causes include the state of the economy, such as a recession; [[Globalization|globalization]] and [[International trade|international trade]] competition; new technologies; government policies; market regulation; and [[War|war]], civil disorder, and [[Natural disaster|natural disasters]]. Economists distinguish several types, including cyclical, frictional, structural, and classical unemployment. Voluntary unemployment reflects individuals' decisions, while involuntary unemployment results from the economic environment, such as workers fired after a company bankruptcy or industrial decline. The International Labour Organization counted 172 million people without work worldwide in 2018, or 5% of the reported global workforce. Because measuring unemployment through surveys or registers is difficult, the employment-to-population ratio is sometimes considered more suitable.

Member of the clade Euungulata, a group of mostly large hoofed mammals. Living ungulates fall into two orders: odd-toed Perissodactyla, including [[Horse|horses]], [[Rhinoceros|rhinoceroses]], and tapirs, and even-toed Artiodactyla, including [[Cattle|cattle]], [[Antelope|antelopes]], [[Pig|pigs]], giraffes, and camels. [[Cetacean|Cetaceans]] such as [[Whale|whales]] and dolphins are also artiodactyls, though they lack hooves. Most ungulates are typically herbivorous, and many use gut bacteria to digest cellulose. The former taxon Ungulata proved polyphyletic on molecular evidence, and true ungulates were reclassified as Euungulata in 2001.

Character encoding standard maintained by the Unicode Consortium, designed to support text in all of the world's digitizable writing systems. Version 18.0 defines 172,808 characters and 175 scripts. It has largely supplanted myriad incompatible legacy character sets and encodes the vast majority of text on the Internet. The standard encodes 3,972 [[Emoji|emoji]]. Unicode text is stored as binary data using one of several encodings; the standard itself defines [[UTF-8|UTF-8]], UTF-16, and UTF-32. UTF-8 is by far the most widely used, partly because of its backward compatibility with [[ASCII|ASCII]].

Legendary creature, described since antiquity as a beast with a single large, spiraling horn projecting from its forehead. Seals of the [[Bronze Age|Bronze Age]] Indus Valley civilization, from around 2000 BC, often show a single-horned animal, though the interpretation remains controversial. The 4th century BC Persian court physician Ctesias described a fleet wild ass from India with a horn a cubit and a half (700 mm, 28 inches) long. In the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]] and [[Renaissance|Renaissance]], European writers portrayed the unicorn as a symbol of purity and grace that could be captured only by a virgin, and its horn was said to make poisoned water potable. The [[Narwhal|narwhal]]'s tusk was sometimes sold as a unicorn horn. Today the unicorn is often a symbol of fantasy or rarity, and in the 21st century it became an LGBTQ symbol.

Abrahamic new religious movement founded in [[Seoul|Seoul]], South Korea, in 1954 by Sun Myung Moon. Members, called Unificationists or informally Moonies, follow the book *Divine Principle*. Moon regarded himself as the [[Second Coming|Second Coming]] of Christ. The church is known for its mass weddings, called Blessing ceremonies, and it promotes anti-[[Communism|communism]] and Korean reunification. Critics have called it a dangerous [[Cult|cult]] and accused it of excessive financial exploitation. The Tokyo High Court upheld a 2025 order to dissolve the church in Japan, and Japan's Supreme Court confirmed the decision in June 2026.

Process of 1866–71 that built the first German nation-state, excluding Austria. It began on August 18, 1866, with the North German Confederation Treaty, a military alliance dominated by the [[Kingdom of Prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]]. It symbolically concluded on January 18, 1871, when the southern German states joined and the [[German Empire|German Empire]], with 25 member states, was proclaimed under Prussian leadership. Legally, the decisive steps were January 1, 1871, when the southern states acceded and the name German Empire was adopted; May 4, 1871, when the permanent constitution took effect; and May 10, 1871, with the Treaty of Frankfurt. Historians debate whether [[Otto von Bismarck|Otto von Bismarck]] had a master plan or simply sought to expand Prussian power. Prussian victories in three regional wars generated national pride that politicians could harness. The Peace of Prague settled the question of a "small Germany" without Austria against a "greater Germany" with it in favor of the former.

Nineteenth-century political and social movement, also called the Risorgimento, that unified most of the Italian Peninsula. For centuries the peninsula had been divided among city-states, kingdoms, and the [[Papal States|Papal States]]. The movement was precipitated by the [[Revolutions of 1848|Revolutions of 1848]]. In 1861 the Kingdom of Sardinia annexed various states to create the [[Kingdom of Italy|Kingdom of Italy]], and Rome, captured in 1870, became capital in 1871. Key figures included King Victor Emmanuel II, statesman [[Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour|Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour]], general [[Giuseppe Garibaldi|Giuseppe Garibaldi]], and journalist Giuseppe Mazzini. Trento and [[Trieste|Trieste]], annexed in 1918 after [[World War I|World War I]], are often considered the culmination of the movement. Italy celebrates the anniversary on March 17, the date the kingdom was proclaimed.

Costume worn by members of an organization while participating in its activities. Uniforms are most often worn by [[Military|armed forces]], paramilitary organizations, [[Police|police]], emergency services, and security guards, and by [[Prison|prison]] inmates. In some countries, officials such as the Commissioned Corps of the United States Public Health Service also wear them on duty. For some organizations, such as the police, it may be illegal for non-members to wear the uniform. Employers use uniforms for branding and a standard corporate image, for workers including [[Bank|bank]] staff, [[Airline|airline]] employees, and bar, restaurant, and hotel employees. Military uniforms are standardized and distinctive, typically a sign of organized forces equipped by a central authority. Many countries require [[School|school]] uniforms, which range from a standard T-shirt to formal wear, though empirical studies show limited direct effects on behavior or achievement. The word derives from the Latin *unus*, meaning "one," and *forma*, meaning "form."

British multinational consumer goods company headquartered in [[London|London]]. It was formed in 1930 by the merger of Dutch margarine producer Margarine Unie and British soapmaker Lever Brothers. It is the largest producer of soap in the world, and its products are sold in over 190 countries. Acquisitions include Lipton (1971) and Ben & Jerry's (2000). Under Paul Polman in the 2010s, the company shifted its focus from food brands toward health and beauty, and it is now focused on health and personal care products. It is listed on the [[London Stock Exchange|London Stock Exchange]] and the [[New York Stock Exchange|New York Stock Exchange]].

National flag of the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]], also called the Union Flag. No law makes it the national flag; it holds that status by precedent. It overlays the red cross of [[Saint George|Saint George]] for England, the white saltire of Saint Andrew for [[Scotland|Scotland]], and the red saltire of Saint Patrick for [[Northern Ireland|Northern Ireland]]. Wales is not represented, because the earlier flag of Great Britain was designed while Wales was part of England. Many [[British Overseas Territories|British Overseas Territories]] and former British possessions incorporate it into their flags. It retains official status in [[Canada|Canada]] as the Royal Union Flag.

Class I freight railroad operating in 23 U.S. states west of [[Chicago|Chicago]] and [[New Orleans|New Orleans]], headquartered in [[Omaha, Nebraska|Omaha, Nebraska]]. It is the second-largest U.S. railroad after BNSF, with 8,300 locomotives over 32,200 miles (51,800 km) of routes. Founded in 1862 as the Union Pacific Rail Road, it built the eastern section of the first transcontinental railroad, which met the Central Pacific line in Utah. The company has announced plans to acquire Norfolk Southern Railway for $85 billion, which would create the first transcontinental railroad network in the United States if approved by regulators.

Set of all elements that belong to at least one set in a given collection. The union of two [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] A and B contains the elements of A, of B, or of both; for example, the union of {1, 3, 5, 7} and {1, 2, 4, 6, 7} is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. The operation is commutative and associative, and it is distributive over [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]]. A nullary union, the union of zero sets, is by definition the [[Empty set|empty set]]. In [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]], the axiom of union guarantees that the union of any collection of sets exists. The union of an arbitrary collection is written ⋃ and is sometimes called an infinitary union.

Japanese casual-wear designer and retailer, wholly owned by Fast Retailing. Its first store opened in Hiroshima in 1984, and it began expanding abroad with stores in the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]] in 2001. Under its LifeWear concept of simple, functional, continually improved [[Clothing|clothing]], the company integrates product planning, production, distribution, and retailing. As of May 31, 2026, Uniqlo operated 2,529 stores worldwide, including 785 in [[Japan|Japan]]. The name was intended as an abbreviation of "unique clothing," but the "C" was reportedly misread as a "Q" while the brand was being registered in [[Hong Kong|Hong Kong]].

Secret biological and chemical warfare research unit of the Imperial Japanese Army, active 1933–45 at [[Harbin|Harbin]] in [[Manchukuo|Manchukuo]]. Led by General Shirō Ishii, it carried out the largest biological weapons attacks in history during the [[Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]], killing an estimated 200,000 people by poisoning water, food, and crops. Human experiments at its facility killed an estimated 14,000 people. After the war, the United States granted Ishii and other personnel immunity in exchange for their research data. A Tokyo court in 2002 held Japan responsible for related deaths but rejected compensation.

Circle of radius 1 centered at the origin of the Cartesian plane. By the [[Pythagorean theorem|Pythagorean theorem]], points (x, y) on it satisfy x² + y² = 1. The cosine and sine of an angle θ are the coordinates of the point where its terminal arm meets the circle, a use that frequently appears in trigonometry. In the [[Complex number|complex plane]], the unit circle is the set of numbers of magnitude one, which form a group under multiplication. In topology it is denoted S¹.

Definite magnitude of a quantity, defined and adopted by convention or law as a standard for measuring that kind of quantity. Any other quantity of that kind is expressed as a multiple of the unit; 10 [[Metre|meters]], for example, is 10 times the predetermined length called the meter. Units were among the earliest human tools, and many early units of length were set by parts of the [[Human body|human body]]. The earliest uniform systems appeared in the 4th and 3rd millennia BC in [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], Egypt, and the Indus Valley. The decimal [[Metric system|metric system]] was developed in France during the [[French Revolution|French Revolution]]. The [[International System of Units|International System of Units]] (SI) is now the global standard, but the United States is the only industrialized country that has not mostly converted to it.

Liberal religious tradition with no single creed, committed to theological diversity, inclusivity, and social justice. Congregations are unified by shared covenants rather than doctrine, and members' beliefs range from [[Atheism|atheism]] to [[Christianity|Christianity]], [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], and other traditions. The Unitarian Universalist Association was formed in 1961 by merging the American Unitarian Association and the Universalist Church of America. Headquartered in [[Boston|Boston]], it serves mostly U.S. congregations. In 2025, about 0.4% of American adults, or roughly 1.4 million people, identified with Unitarian Universalism, according to the Public Religion Research Institute.
